title: Transfer Functions, Poles and Zeros
question: Can we read a system's whole personality off one fraction?

blocks.text: Start the drone hovering at 1 m, with 4.9 N of base thrust balancing gravity. Measure both the requested change and the actual height change from that baseline. Just before a new request, both changes are zero. In the step example the request jumps to 2 m at $t=0$, so its change becomes 1 m while the drone is still at 1 m.

$\Delta\sp{R}(s)$ is the transform of the **requested change** from 1 m; $\Delta\out{H}(s)$ is the transform of the **actual change** from 1 m. $G(s)$ is fixed by the drone and controller. It is the **transfer function**: output change divided by input change, with both changes starting at zero.
The plot still shows heights above the ground. Add the 1 m starting height to a change predicted by the formula to get the blue height on the plot.
So $G(s)$ is like the drone's **recipe**. Feed in any ingredient and it tells you what comes out!
Try three different inputs on the same drone. The recipe never changes, only $\Delta\sp{R}(s)$ does.

items.def: Transformed output change ÷ transformed input change, starting from the same resting state. For this linear drone it is a fraction of polynomials in $s$.

sections.title: Poles: where the system wants to live

blocks.text: Where does $G(s)$ **blow up**? At a zero of its denominator, after any common factors have been canceled. Those points are the **poles**, drawn as ×. In this drone there are two, matching the two natural $e^{st}$ motions from Chapter 6.

blocks.tex: \begin{aligned} & m s^2 + (c + \eff{K_d})\,s + \eff{K_p} = 0 \\ \Longrightarrow\quad & s = p,\ \bar p \qquad \text{(the poles)} \end{aligned}

blocks.text: Now flip it around. Instead of choosing gains and finding the poles, let's **drag the poles** and see what drone we get. (Behind the scenes we work out the controller that puts them there. It needs a new knob $\eff{K_d}$, a push against speed, which we'll meet properly in Chapter 9.)

blocks.q: What does the drone do if we drag the poles into the **right half** of the s-plane?

options.why: Landing needs everything to calm down, and right-half poles do the opposite.
Steady wobbling is what you get exactly **on** the vertical axis. Just past it, things grow.

options.text: It swings harder and harder until it crashes or flies off
options.why: On the right half, $e^{st}$ has $\sigma > 0$: a growing spiral. The swings get bigger every cycle.

blocks.text: Play with it. A few rules jump out, and they're all Chapter 5 and 6 in disguise:

items: **Left half = calms down, right half = blows up.** The real part $\sigma$ is the shrink or grow rate.
**Further left = faster.** Settling takes about $4/|\sigma|$ seconds (the dashed vertical lines).
**Further up = more wiggly.** The height $\omega$ is the wiggle speed; one wiggle takes $2\pi/\omega$ seconds.
**The angle sets the overshoot.** Poles near the real axis barely overshoot, poles near the vertical axis overshoot a lot (the dashed rays).

blocks.text: I wanted just **one** pole up high and one down low. It won't let me! The bottom one keeps copying the top one.
Remember the twin spinners from Chapter 5? A real drone has real motion, so every spinning $e^{st}$ needs its mirror twin to cancel the imaginary parts. Complex poles **always** come in mirror pairs.
Our drone started at $-1 \pm 6.24i$: that's the $K_p = 20$ drone from Chapter 2. Far up (very wiggly) and close to the axis (slow to settle). Now you can *see* why it bounced.

The numerator can be zero too. Those points are **zeros**, drawn as ○. Usually they change **how much** of each pole’s motion appears in the output. If a zero sits exactly on a pole, the shared factor cancels and that pole disappears from this input-to-output transfer function. An internal motion can still remain hidden from that particular input and output.

Here's a system with fixed poles at $-2 \pm 3i$ and one zero you can slide. (You get exactly this shape from a controller that reacts to how fast the *error* changes, which is a teaser for Chapter 9.)
Same poles, but when the zero gets close to the origin the response jumps up way faster and overshoots more!

A zero near the origin makes the system react strongly to **changes** in the input. The overshoot grows, even though the poles didn't move. Far away, the zero hardly matters. That's all we need about zeros for now.
Easy: drag the poles *way* left. Settles in a blink. Best drone ever!
What thrust does that need, though? Until now we've pretended the motors could push as hard as the maths wants.

Time to be honest. Our motors can push between **0 N** and **20 N** (about four times the drone's weight). Below, the poles move left along a 45° line. The dashed curves are the maths with imaginary, unlimited motors; the solid ones are real motors.

Past a certain point the maths demands 50, 60, 70 newtons that the motors simply don't have. The {eff|orange thrust} flattens against the limits, the real drone stops following the pretty linear prediction, and it overshoots *more* than it would with gentler poles.
So "further left" is only better until you run out of motor. Placing poles is a trade-off, not a race.
From now on the 20 N limit stays switched on.

items: The **transfer function** $G(s)$ = output ÷ input in s-land. It's the system's recipe: $\out{H} = G\cdot\sp{R}$.
**Poles** (×) are where $G(s)$ explodes: the $e^{st}$ terms the system is made of.
Left half = stable, right half = explodes, further left = faster (≈ 4/|σ| s), higher = wigglier, angle = overshoot.
Complex poles always come in mirror pairs.
**Zeros** (○) change how much of each term you get. Near the origin they add a kick.
Far-left poles need thrust the motors don't have.

options.why: Settling ≈ $4/1 = 4$ s. The height (2) only affects wiggling, not settling.
High up means lots of fast wiggles, but it's close to the axis, so they die out slowly (≈ 8 s).

items.q: $G(s) = \dfrac{3}{s^2 + 2s + 10}$. Where are the poles, and what does the response look like?

options.why: $s = \frac{-2 \pm \sqrt{4 - 40}}{2} = -1 \pm 3i$. Left half means stable, imaginary part means wiggles.
Sign slip. For $s^2 + bs + c$ the real part is $-b/2 = -1$, which is in the left half.
Those are just coefficients of the polynomial. The poles are its roots: $-1 \pm 3i$.

items.q: You want **less overshoot** but the **same settling time**. How do you move the poles?

options.text: Straight towards the real axis (keep σ, shrink ω)
options.why: Same distance from the axis means same settling time. A smaller angle from the real axis means more damping, so less overshoot.
That swings the angle towards the vertical axis: *more* overshoot and faster wiggles.
That makes it settle more slowly, and past the axis it becomes unstable.

items.q: Poles at $+0.5 \pm 2i$. What do you see?

options.why: $\sigma = +0.5 > 0$ means growth, $\omega = 2$ means spinning: a growing wiggle.
Shrinking needs $\sigma < 0$ (left half). These poles are on the right.
That's exactly on the axis ($\sigma = 0$). At $+0.5$ it grows.

blocks.text: Theo: "The poles are beautiful. But hold on: we cheated all chapter by handing the drone its hover thrust. Without it, gravity still makes it **droop**. Our map is fine. It's our *controller* that needs fixing."

recipe.title: One recipe, three inputs
recipe.plotAria: Setpoint and drone height over time for the chosen input.

describe.step: The setpoint steps from 1 to 2 metres and the drone follows with a bouncy overshoot.
describe.pulse: The setpoint glides from 1 to 2 metres; the drone follows with a smaller bounce.
describe.wave: The setpoint waves up and down; the drone follows the wave.

playground.title: The pole playground
playground.planeAria: The s-plane with a draggable pair of poles. Left half calms down, right half blows up. Use arrow keys to move the selected pole.
playground.plotAria: Step response of the drone for the chosen poles, previous response shown as a ghost.

verdict.marginal: Right on the axis: it swings forever.
verdict.hitPage: It flew out of its picture, hit the page, and fell. Move a pole to try again.

playground.challenge: Mini-challenge: overshoot under 10% and settled within 2 s
playground.chalOk: Challenge met! Overshoot {o}%, settled in {s} s.
playground.chalNo: Not yet: overshoot {o}%, settles in {s} s. Aim for the highlighted zone.
playground.help: Drag either × (or Tab to it and use the arrow keys, Shift for big steps). The drone replays its step response each time.
playground.describe: Poles at {p}. Damping ratio {z}. Settles in about {s} seconds, overshoots about {o} percent.

zero.title: Slide the zero
zero.planeAria: The s-plane with two fixed poles at minus 2 plus or minus 3 i and a draggable zero on the real axis.
zero.plotAria: Step responses with and without the zero.
zero.near: Near the origin: a big early kick and extra overshoot.
zero.far: Far away: the zero barely changes anything.
zero.help: Drag the ○ along the axis (or Tab to it and use ← →). The × poles stay put.

limit.title: Real motors have limits
limit.hAria: Height after a step for unlimited and for real motors.
limit.tAria: Thrust over time, with the 0 and 20 newton motor limits.
limit.capped: The maths wants {p} N, but the motors top out at 20 N. Reality stops following the linear picture.
limit.fantasy: Imaginary motors happily deliver {p} N. Switch the limits back on.
limit.fine: Within the motors' range: maths and reality agree.
